title: South Africa coach Rassie Erasmus banned for six games over ‘match-fixing’ outburst
content:
South Africa rugby union head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended from taking charge of the Springboks for six games after he questioned the integrity of match officials.

The 54-year-old has been banned by an independent panel under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process after he made a series of controversial claims in a press conference in the wake of his side’s 21-19 defeat to France last Friday.

Erasmus, who has led South Africa to two World Cup triumphs and is widely regarded as the outstanding, and controversial, rugby coach of his generation, said he did not think Ireland’s Sam Prendergast would be banned despite being cited for a tackle during the first half of the game between Ireland and Fiji in the Nations Championship on Saturday.

The Springboks are set to face Ireland in Dublin on Saturday in a Nations Championship clash, with a place in the final at Twickenham on November 29 at stake. South Africa are currently second in the Southern Hemisphere series table, two points behind New Zealand ahead of the finals weekend.

“I must say the right words now. We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play,” Erasmus told reporters concerning Prendergast. “I’m not saying anybody’s doing anything wrong. I’m just not expecting him to get (suspended) — I think he’ll play on Saturday.”

In his press conference on Monday, widely reported by media, he asked if “manipulation of the game” or “match-fixing” were behind some foul play going unpenalised during games, including his team’s loss in Paris.

“There’s 17 knee-drop tackles and the TMO (Italy’s Matteo Liperini) doesn’t come in once,” said Erasmus. “I’m not saying he’s wrong, I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?

“Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it’s been decided that knee-drop tackles are out.

“On numerous times, we mentioned to the referee (Andrea Piardi, also from Italy), ‘We think there’s (been) a knee-drop tackle’. And if the TMO didn’t see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to?”

South Africa Rugby has requested a full disciplinary hearing for Erasmus. In a statement, a spokesperson said that the organisation “respected the process” but had asked that Erasmus be allowed to “contextualise his comments” and that “it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives”.

It added that it hopes the hearing can be expedited due to the seriousness of the charge. The next step for the Springboks would be to provide their formal submissions to World Rugby, who would then need to convene a new panel to hear the appeal case.

At present, the sanction would mean that Erasmus cannot have “any matchday involvement”, ranging from coaching and “any contact with team management or players on matchday”, along with a series of other restrictions, according to World Rugby’s ruling.

Given the Springboks next game is on Saturday, it remains to be seen if the process will take place in time for Erasmus to take charge at the Aviva Stadium.

In its statement, World Rugby added: “Respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport. Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously. Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.

“Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official’s integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse.”

This is far from the first time that Erasmus has fallen foul of governing bodies during a colourful, and supremely successful, coaching career.

He was banned for two months by World Rugby in 2021 for criticising the refereeing during South Africa’s defeat by the British and Irish Lions in their first Test.

He also fulfilled the role of ‘water boy’ in the same series, as a means of passing on instructions to his players during the match. His behaviour led to a change in regulations by World Rugby, banning coaches from carrying water onto the field.

Erasmus, 54, has also regularly aired grievances against match officials on social media, leading to criticism from former international referee Nigel Owens.

“We don’t need that in the game and I’d have thought he’d have learned his lesson by now,” he told The Telegraph in 2022. “Once you start putting things out there on social media questioning decisions, that’s not what this game is about.”
